content:
Which department decided that residents cannot return to Wang Fuk Court?

During the Q&A session, multiple owners raised this issue. At least five speakers questioned Hop On (the property management company) about which department had made the decision to bar residents from returning to Wang Fuk Court and what legal basis underpinned the lockdown. Hop On avoided giving a direct answer on the first four occasions, merely stating that Wang Fuk Court remained under lockdown and that the matter fell outside the manager's authority to arrange, and advising owners in need to contact the one-household-one-social-worker service — prompting heckling from owners at several venues.

Hop On unaware of legal basis for the lockdown

Solicitor Leung Ping-chiu eventually responded that Hop On did not know on what legal basis the authorities had imposed the lockdown, and it would be inappropriate to explain on their behalf in case it misinterpreted the government's considerations. As for the survey reports on the other seven buildings of Wang Fuk Court, which also drew much attention, Hop On said a typhoon and rainy season were approaching and the reports might be released once the authorities completed their inspections. Hop On also said that after taking legal advice, it considered the demands to fall outside its responsibilities as manager.

Owners concerned government using donations to acquire titles, not rebuilding to save compensation for China Taiping?

The government has already stated it will not rebuild on the original site. At the meeting, several owners worried this meant the HK$2 billion 'fire insurance' payout based on the cost of restoring the building's structure would not be honoured: 'Is the government using donations to take back the titles and not rebuilding so as to save compensation for China Taiping?' A representative of China Taiping Insurance (Hong Kong), Ms Lau, said that once the policy liability was established, the company would pay out according to the policy terms regardless of whether repair or rebuilding took place, and that any acquisition would not affect the policy liability or the calculation of the amount. However, Ms Lau also said the specific policy and legal liability could only be further assessed after the independent committee and various government departments had completed their investigations and announced the results.

Wang Chi House repairs estimated at HK$30 million

Hop On also gave an update on Wang Chi House, which was not affected by the fire. Earlier, Hop On had said repairs to Wang Chi House would cost at least HK$30 million and take at least nine months, involving re-tiling of external walls and electrical repairs. Today, Hop On revised the total to about HK$32 million, with a construction period of three to nine months. Solicitor Leung Ping-chiu, invited by Hop On to attend the meeting, noted that Wang Chi House formed part of the entire estate under the Deed of Mutual Covenant, and separating it out would require substantial amendments to the DMC with the consent of all owners — a complicated and costly procedure.

Owners question Hop On for failing to convene owners' meeting within statutory period while successfully issuing subsidy cheques on behalf of URA earlier this year, demanding 'What's so difficult about finding us owners for a meeting?' Hop On's Property Services Director Chan Wai-kwong, who chaired the meeting, did not answer directly, saying it was a venue issue — finding a venue that could accommodate a thousand residents was genuinely difficult, and only after the Home Affairs Department provided a venue could the meeting be held. An owner criticised the explanation as unreasonable: 'Hong Kong hosts so many of those mega-event economy shows that easily pack tens of thousands into a venue. Telling me you can't find a place for our 2,000 people is really a hard sell. I hope you won't use that as an excuse again.'
